entities.summary:
Antonio Lombardo (c.1458–1516) was an Italian Renaissance sculptor who gained recognition for his work in the Vatican, specifically in the creation of the 'Theological Beasts' for the Sistine Chapel's frescoes. His artistic skills were likely shaped by his apprenticeship under Baldassare Peruzzi and his training in humanist ideals. Lombardo's influence extended to the development of Renaissance sculpture, as his designs were studied and emulated by later artists. His work also reflects the cultural and artistic exchange between Italy and other European countries during the 15th and 16th centuries. The artistic community of Florence was likely familiar with Lombardo's work, and his sculptures can be seen as an important part of the city's rich artistic heritage.

Lombardo's death in 1516 marked the end of an era for Italian Renaissance art, and his legacy continued to inspire artists well into the 17th century. His innovative use of classical motifs and his focus on the human form paved the way for future sculptors to experiment with new techniques and styles.

The exact dates of Lombardo's birth and death are unknown, but it is known that he was active in Rome during the early 16th century. His sculptures are a testament to the enduring power of art to transcend time and culture.
